content: Gaucher disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. This condition is unique among ultra-rare diseases because there are currently four approved treatments available for routine clinical use. Historically, due to the limited number of affected individuals worldwide and the lack of alternative therapies to imiglucerase for an extended period, these treatments have not been rigorously evaluated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which are now considered the gold standard for generating high-quality clinical evidence. The objective of this review was to compile and analyze all available RCT data on the efficacy and safety of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and substrate reduction therapy (SRT) for Gaucher disease. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, and reference lists of relevant articles. The last search was performed on August 7, 2014. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled studies (including open-label and cross-over designs) that evaluated ERT or SRT in any type of Gaucher disease. Two independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias and extracted relevant data from the included studies. Out of 488 studies identified, eight met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 300 participants. The primary outcomes assessed included hemoglobin concentration, platelet count, spleen and liver volume, and serum biomarkers such as chitotriosidase and CCL18. Only one study demonstrated a low risk of bias across all parameters. All included studies were randomized. Four studies evaluated the effects of ERT in previously untreated individuals with type 1 Gaucher disease. Two studies focused on maintenance ERT in patients with stable type 1 Gaucher disease who had been treated for at least two years. One study compared SRT, ERT, and a combination of both as maintenance therapy in individuals with type 1 Gaucher disease previously treated with ERT. Another study investigated SRT in patients with chronic neuronopathic (type 3) Gaucher disease who were also receiving ERT. In treatment-naïve participants, similar increases in hemoglobin levels were observed across various ERT regimens, including imiglucerase or alglucerase at 60 units/kg, imiglucerase or velaglucerase alfa at 60 units/kg, taliglucerase alfa at 30 or 60 units/kg, and velaglucerase alfa at 45 or 60 units/kg. For platelet count responses in participants with intact spleens, imiglucerase showed a benefit over velaglucerase alfa at 60 units/kg, with a mean difference of -79.87 (95% confidence interval: -137.57 to -22.17). No significant differences in platelet count responses were observed when comparing other ERT regimens or doses. Reductions in spleen and liver volumes were comparable across all ERT products and doses. While no dose-dependent effects on serum biomarkers were observed at nine months, a significantly greater reduction was noted with higher doses after 12 months in the velaglucerase alfa study, with a mean difference of 16.70 (95% confidence interval: 1.51 to 31.89). In two maintenance ERT studies comparing infusions every two weeks versus every four weeks, no significant differences were found in hemoglobin concentration, platelet count, or spleen and liver volumes over a 6to 12-month period when participants received the same cumulative dose. A total of 25 serious adverse events were reported, most of which were deemed unrelated to treatment. No RCTs of SRT in treatment-naïve patients were available for evaluation. However, miglustat monotherapy appeared to be as effective as continued ERT in maintaining hematological, organ, and biomarker responses in individuals with type 1 Gaucher disease who had been treated with imiglucerase for at least two years. In patients with neuronopathic Gaucher disease, adding miglustat to ERT did not result in significant improvements in hemoglobin concentration, platelet count, or organ volumes. One RCT assessing SRT was published shortly before the finalization of this review, and another ongoing study is expected to be published soon. These studies will be evaluated in future updates of the review. The authors concluded that the analysis highlights the challenges of relying solely on RCTs for evidence in rare chronic diseases like Gaucher disease. During the first year of treatment, different recombinant glucocerebrosidases were found to be bio-similar and non-inferior in terms of safety and efficacy for surrogate biological response parameters. ERT at doses of 30 to 45 units/kg every two to four weeks was generally as effective as the 60 units/kg dose for the clinical outcomes assessed. The findings underscore the need for innovative trial designs and methodologies to generate robust data on the long-term efficacy and safety of treatments for rare diseases. This is particularly important for understanding the sustained disease-modifying effects of therapies in individuals with chronic conditions like Gaucher disease.
